paper_title: Depth-adaptive Inference of Looped Language Models via Continuous Depth Batching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A main promise of looped language models is depth-adaptive inference. By looping a block of shared layers a variable number of times, the model can use less compute for "easy" tokens and more for "hard" ones. However, tokens with different numbers of loops cannot share a uniform forward pass and therefore cannot be handled by standard batching systems such as vLLM. The practical value of depth-adaptive inference thus hinges on whether batching can be made efficient. We introduce the first efficient method for depth-adaptive looped LMs via continuous depth batching (CDB), which forms new batches between loop steps. Our method dynamically schedules looped and non-looped parts of the architecture, manages looped KV-caching, and predicts which tokens will exit the loop in advance so it can prepare batches asynchronously. Experiments on Ouro 1.4B and Huginn 3.5B show that fully looped architectures are best suited to depth-adaptive inference, as large non-looped layers outside the recurrent core (e.g., token embedding, LM head, and unshared transformer blocks) slow down and complicate scheduling. Overall, CDB realizes up to 99% of the estimated maximum speedup available, leaving further gains primarily dependent on model architecture and exit behavior.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Batching, i.e., processing multiple sequences in one forward pass, is central to large language model (LLM) inference. Online APIs, reinforcement learning, and benchmarking require processing many sequences at once. Batching is especially important for autoregressive decoding, which generates responses one token at time. Without batching, each decode step loads the model weights from memory to process single token. Weight loading often takes much longer than the computation, leaving compute units underutilized; the forward pass is memory-bandwidth bound (Anthony et al., 2024). By processing multiple sequences, batching reuses the loaded weights and turns small matrix multiplications into larger, more efficient ones. With large enough batch, the forward pass can even become compute bound, saturating the compute units while weight-loading time becomes negligible. Hardware constraints and inference systems also increasingly influence LLM architecture design (Anthony et al., 2024; Bian et al., 2026). For example, layer dimensions are chosen based on accelerator utilization, modern attention layers reduce KV-cache memory footprint, and native multi-token prediction enables self-speculative decoding (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Gloeckle et al., 2024). Looped language models, however, have received little attention from the inference perspective, despite offering several potential advantages. looped LM repeatedly applies block of shared layers, called the recurrent core, to refine the latent representation before predicting token. Sharing layers reduces parameter memory relative to an equally deep standard transformer and also makes it possible to reuse KV states across depth (Geiping et al., 2025). The key advantage we focus on is depth-adaptive decoding, which allows tokens to exit the recurrent core after different depths (Fig. 1, left) (Dehghani et al., 2019; Graves, 2017). The model spends fewer loops and less compute on easy tokens, and more loops on hard ones, improving the computeaccuracy trade-off (Zhu et al., 2025). However, the compute savings from depth-adaptive decoding do not automatically translate into faster inference. The central challenge is that tokens with different numbers of loops cannot share 1 Preprint. CDB removes tokens from the loop as they exit and refills the freed slots with new tokens to keep batch size large (Fig. 1, right). However, this makes scheduling much more complex and naive implementation can incur more overhead than early exit saves, leaving standard fixed-depth batching faster. In this work, we ask: Can depth-adaptive looped LMs be served efficiently? Which architectural properties determine their speedup? For this, we introduce the first end-to-end CDB implementation, addressing several open challenges. Looped LMs contain boundary stages outside the shared core that run only once and must be scheduled alongside changing loop batches: the prelude processes each token before it enters the loop, and the coda predicts the next token after it exits (Fig. 1, left). New tokens for refilling freed batch slots are also not directly available: the next token of an exit needs to pass through coda and prelude and new request must first complete prompt prefill and prelude. Furthermore, exit decisions become available only after loop step finishes, so the scheduler cannot prepare the next recurrent batch in advance, leaving the GPU idle. To address these challenges, we interleave prefill, prelude, and coda batches with loop steps, allowing new and exiting sequences to provide replacement tokens for refill, and use lookahead gate to overlap batch preparation with GPU execution. We implement the original refill scheduler and simpler no-refill mode that only removes tokens (Fig. 1, right). To analyze CDB, we derive prefill-corrected speedup estimate and hardware-aware latency model that predicts when refill helps. We evaluate CDB in offline throughput and online serving benchmarks on two prominent looped architectures. Our results show that refill is important, especially in the memory-bound regime and for fully looped models such as Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025), whose boundary stages are minimal. On Ouro, CDB realizes up to 99% of the estimated maximum speedup available from early exit. For Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025), costly transformer boundary stages increase the cost of refill and no-refill performs better. Here, CDB realizes 83 to 96% of the available speedup. Contributions. 1. We enable efficient depth-adaptive inference for looped LMs with the first end-to-end implementation of CDB. 2. We compare theoretical compute savings with wall-clock speed-up by deriving FLOPbased upper bound and hardware-aware model of recurrent-step latency. 3. We show how boundary-stage cost, KV cache design, and loop count determine inference efficiency, providing concrete guidance for inference-aware looped-LM architecture design.

sections.title: 2 PROBLEM SETUP
sections.content: The looped-LM architecture is split into prelude Pθ, shared recurrent core Rθ, and coda Cθ. rmax times, while the prelude and coda each run once. For token t, the recurrent core runs rt 2 Preprint. We denote the number of transformer layers in these stages as prelude-core-coda. For example, 2-4-2 model executes 2+4rt+2 layers, giving an effective depth of 20 at rt=4 loops. fully looped 0-4-0 model has no transformer layers outside the core; its boundary stages (i.e., prelude and coda) only contain the embedding layer and LM head. Within this architecture, depth-adaptive decoding lets rt vary per token: after each loop, an exit criterion determines whether the token stops looping. Crucially, each token leaves the core at an input-dependent depth, decided at the end of loop step. This per-token variability creates problem for batched inference. Standard continuous batching (CB) schedules only at token boundaries: at each tick, active sequences generate one token, completed sequences are removed, and new sequences are admitted (Yu et al., 2022). Because CB treats the complete forward pass as one scheduling unit, every token in batch must execute the same operations. With adaptive depth, however, an exited token must run the coda while the remaining tokens may require another loop step. To support this, the CDB scheduler must operate within the forward pass by tracking each tokens loop progress individually and routing tokens between stages as they exit. Overall, CDB must address three main challenges: (1) stage heterogeneitya CB step is one uniform forward pass, while CDB must schedule prefill, prelude, recurrent core, and coda separately, each at different batch sizes and frequencies; (2) missing KV stateswhen token exits at rt, it writes no KV states for deeper loop steps, leaving later tokens without state to attend to if they loop deeper; (3) critical-path exitsthe exit decision is available only after step but determines which tokens enter step + 1, so the GPU idles after each loop step until the scheduler has processed the exit.

sections.title: 3 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Depth-adaptive looped transformers. We focus on methods that decide for each token individually when it leaves the loop. Here, learned variants attach small exit head to the recurrent core (Banino et al., 2021; Frey et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025), while training-free variants compare latent states or output logits between consecutive loop steps and exit once they converge (Geiping et al., 2025; Kohli et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). In contrast, in Mixture-of-Depths-style methods, tokens exit in fixed-sized groups (Bae et al., 2025b; Mohtashami et al., 2025; Raposo et al., 2024), while in sequence-level methods, all tokens exit at the same depth (Jeddi et al., 2026; Prairie et al., 2026). We study per-token adaptive depth from systems perspective, quantifying how its FLOP savings translate into throughput and latency gains. Importantly, CDB does not change the models predictions and exit decisions. Depth-adaptive standard transformers. Early exit has also been studied for standard transformers, where intermediate layers can predict the next token and stop computation early (Elbayad et al., 2020; Elhoushi et al., 2024; Schuster et al., 2022; Yoo et al., 2026). However, efficient batched inference remains difficult because their unshared layers prevent refill across depths and leave missing KV states that must be recomputed or approximated when needed (Bae et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Corro et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Shen & Zou, 2026). We study CDB only for looped LMs, as their shared recurrent core naturally allows cross-depth refill and KV sharing without recomputation. Continuous depth batching. Bae et al. (2025a) introduced CDB for looped LMs theoretically and estimated its throughput speedup through simulation. Bae et al. (2025b) later evaluated CDB in ablation experiments, excluding prefill, scheduling, and KV-cache updates. In contrast, we include all of these costs and provide the first end-to-end implementation and evaluation of CDB.

sections.title: 4 METHOD: CONTINUOUS DEPTH BATCHING
sections.content: 4.1 STAGE-WISE SCHEDULING We conceptually split each requests path from prompt to completed response into four queues: inactive requests waiting for prefill, decode tokens awaiting the prelude, recurrent items ready for their next loop step, and exited tokens awaiting the coda. These queues correspond to the four stages of looped inference, which can be batched and run separately. In principle, the scheduler can execute them in any order, allowing prefill, prelude, recurrent, and coda batches to be interleaved. Based on this queuing system, we implement two execution modes that differ in how the stages are ordered. Exited tokens are removed from the recurrent batch, reducing batch size and thus compute on subsequent loop steps. In refill mode (Algorithm 2), the scheduler orders the stages dynamically so that freed slots can be filled by new tokens, keeping batch size high. For refill, we use priority rule to determine the dynamic order. We let prelude run directly after prefill or coda, as there is no routing decision between these stages. Among the remaining stages, coda has highest priority because it predicts next tokens for refill and finishing requests. Prefill comes next, since admitting prompts early allows for larger decode batches. Otherwise, we run the recurrent core. Without an additional constraint, this priority system would run the coda after every individual exit. For models with costly coda layers, repeatedly running them on only few tokens can outweigh the benefit of refill. We therefore introduce minimum coda batch size K: coda takes priority only after at least exits have accumulated. See implementation details in Appendix A. With refill (K=1), coda and prelude run immediately for the single exited token, so the next recurrent batch refills to B=64. With refill (K=16), the recurrent batch first continues with 63 tokens, allowing more exits to accumulate before coda and prelude run on 30 tokens together. No-refill waits until the entire recurrent batch has exited and processes all 64 tokens through the coda together. larger therefore makes coda and prelude batches more efficient, but delays refill and temporarily reduces the recurrent batch size, making it less efficient. Complete scheduling traces are provided in Appendix A.4. 4.2 DEPTH-AWARE KV CACHE depth-indexed KV cache gives each shared layer separate slot for every loop step, resulting in rmax slots per token. When token exits early (rt<rmax), its remaining slots stay empty, but later tokens reaching these loop steps need state to attend to. We consider two ways to provide these missing states (Fig. 2, right), both compatible with modern attention kernels like paged attention (Kwon et al., 2023) and FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022). last-exited cache copies tokens final KV state into skipped slots upon exit. This generally preserves accuracy and avoids computing the missing states (Zhu et al., 2025), but retains rmax slots and adds copying overhead. shared cache instead gives each recurrent layer single KV slot per token, reducing recurrent-core KV memory by factor of rmax. Each loop step overwrites this slot, so later tokens always attend to the most recent state of each earlier token, regardless of its exit depth. This avoids empty slots and copying, but may require specialized training to preserve accuracy (Geiping et al., 2025; Vendrell et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025). 4.3 ASYNCHRONOUS SCHEDULING CDB introduces frequent CPU interactions between short GPU stages, because CDB schedules every loop and boundary stage separately. After each stage, the scheduler reads back results, selects the next stage, assembles its batch, and transfers the required inputs to the GPU. Doing this synchronously results in much GPU idle time. However, there is problem with preparing the next batch in advance: the gate output at loop step determines which tokens leave the batch, but is only available once step finishes on the GPU. The CPU must read back the result and build the batch before the GPU can start step r+1. End-ofsequence (EOS) tokens pose an analogous problem on the token level, which is usually handled by assuming no EOS and catching it one step late, causing one extra generated token. Unlike the EOS approach, this does not waste compute, since we decide the exit earlier instead of catching it later. In Appendix E.2, we show that the exit decision can be made one step earlier without reducing accuracy. Overall, our CDB implementation reduces GPU idle time to nearly zero (Fig. 3, right).

sections.title: 6 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate CDB in two settings. Offline throughput measures how fast the engine processes fixed workload where all requests are known upfront, as in benchmarking or RL. This sustained load lets us test how much of the estimated maximum speedup CDB can realize and whether the recurrent-step latency model predicts well when refill helps. Online serving replays requests with dynamic arrivals, simulating user queries that arrive at different times, adding queueing effects and varying load. 6.1 SETUP We construct three request workloads with different prompt and output lengths: Alpaca (short instructions) (Taori et al., 2023) , ShareGPT (chat requests with similar average prompt and output lengths) (ShareGPT Team, 2023), and ArXiv-Summarization (long, prefill-heavy prompts) (Cohan et al., 2018). Varying prompt and output lengths tests CDB across different prefill costs, decode durations, and context lengths, all of which affect end-to-end speedup. We also vary each models exit threshold to change how often tokens leave the recurrent core and open slots for refill. For each workload and exit threshold, we set the requests output length to that of their reference responses and replay exit decisions recorded in advance from the models exit policy (Appendix C). We evaluate CDB on the two main looped LM architecture families, i.e., fully looped models and models with transformer layers in their prelude and coda. Ouro 1.4B (Zhu et al., 2025) is fully looped (0-24-0, rmax=4): all its transformer layers are looping, with only the token embedding and LM head outside the recurrent core. Huginn 3.5B (Geiping et al., 2025) has 2-4-2 preludecorecoda split (rmax=16), so 50% of its transformer layers are outside the core. This contrast tests how boundary stages affect the efficiency of depth-adaptive inference and which architecture design is better suited for it. Unless stated otherwise, we set the minimum coda batch size to K=1 for Ouro and K=W/4 for Huginn, where is the maximum number of active sequences (e.g., K=16 at =64). We compare CDB using no-refill and refill against standard token-level CB, which runs rmax loops for every token. All schedulers use the same codebase, kernels, and admission policy, build on Hugging Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2020), vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024). All experiments run on single 80 GB H100 GPU. See Appendix for further details. Preprint. Running the coda immediately allows generated tokens to directly refill free core slots. Waiting for more exits improves coda efficiency at the cost of smaller recurrent batches. What if Huginn had smaller boundary stages? Removing transformer layers from Huginns boundary stages makes immediate coda execution more competitive and improves throughput. For fully looped 0-4-0 split, K=1 is near optimal, mirroring the behavior of Ouro. The gap to the maximum speedup also closes, confirming that boundary-stage cost is central efficiency constraint. sections.title: 7 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Does depth-adaptive decoding result in faster inference? CDB realizes up to 99% of the estimated maximum speedup available from the models early-exit behavior. However, several conditions must hold to make inference meaningfully faster. First, more aggressive exit thresholds and missing KV states can reduce accuracy, so the model must be trained to provide enough early exits at the desired accuracy to create compute savings that CDB can use (Appendix E). Second, recurrent computation must account for sufficient part of total inference time. For example, expensive prefill limits the end-to-end speedup, as our prefill-corrected bound shows. Third, the inference system must turn skipped recurrent computation into lower wall-clock time. In the memory-bound regime, shrinking the recurrent batch saves FLOPs but little time, making refill important. Additionally, updating batches between loop steps frequently stalls the GPU, so an asynchronous system is needed. Overall, our CDB implementation provides the inference method needed, while further inference speedups come from future models that allow more frequent exits at high accuracy. Co-designing looped LMs and inference systems. Our results offer concrete guidance for designing looped models that benefit even more from depth-adaptive inference. Refilling batches between loops can substantially increase inference speed by replacing tokens as they exit. However, refill needs tokens waiting in the recurrent queue, and tokens only get there after running the boundary stages. If those stages are costly, they cannot run as often, leaving fewer tokens ready for refill. This suggests keeping non-looped stages small for efficient inference. However, adding layers outside the recurrent core can improve accuracy (Bae et al., 2025b; Geiping et al., 2025), creating trade-off between accuracy and inference efficiency. Furthermore, more loops offer finer-grained control over exit depths, but each skipped loop then saves smaller fraction of total recurrent compute (Section 5). Higher recurrence counts can also reduce accuracy at matched training compute (Schwethelm et al., 2026). The KV cache layout creates another co-design requirement. Early exits leave KV slots for skipped loops unwritten, requiring policy for missing states. Reusing the last available state avoids recomputation, and looped models can often tolerate this without additional training, though support for KV sharing is not guaranteed. fully shared cache further reduces the memory footprint and implementation complexity of CDB (Appendix E.1). Understanding when these layouts work, and designing models that reliably support them, is an important direction for future work. Designing exit gates. Existing gates make exit decisions from the latest recurrent state, while asynchronous batch preparation requires knowing exits one loop in advance. Our lookahead gate provides this early decision without reducing accuracy, but constrains the minimum exit depth to rmin=2 (Appendix E.2). For Ouro and Huginn, excluding exits after only one loop is consistent with their exit behavior, so the constraint does not reduce their realistic speedup. However, the constraint could reduce the available speedup of models that produce useful outputs after single loop. One solution is to predict the complete exit depth before the token enters the recurrent core. However, making this decision reliable remains difficult (Bae et al., 2025b). more promising alternative is to predict only the first loop-exit before the recurrent core and then use lookahead decisions for all later loops. This would allow rmin=1 without requiring the complete exit depth to be known beforehand. Limitations. We evaluate only two looped architectures on single H100 GPU. Future looped models may introduce components such as mixture-of-experts that change the costs and scheduling requirements of recurrent and boundary stages. Our experiments also do not include production serving features such as multi-GPU execution, preemption, prefix caching, or speculative decoding. These techniques may shift the balance between prefill and decoding or introduce new interactions with depth-adaptive scheduling, so the relative benefit of CDB may differ in broader serving system.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced the first efficient inference method for depth-adaptive looped LMs. Our implementation of continuous depth batching (CDB) decomposes decode steps into separate stage queues, solving the batching problem posed by variable-depth forward passes. Our method is near-optimal and realizes most of the speedup available from early exits, showing that depth-adaptive decoding can be served efficiently. We also give new impulses for looped architecture design to improve the compute accuracy trade-off, e.g., more accurate early exits and less expensive boundary stages. Overall, co-designing looped architectures and serving systems can lead to substantially faster inference. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 INFERENCE SYSTEM OVERVIEW Engine design. Our CB and CDB implementations share the same basic inference design. Each sequence progresses from prefill to autoregressive decode and remains active until generation finishes or the scheduler preempts it. Following SGLangs default setting1 (Zheng et al., 2024), the scheduler forms separate prefill and decode batches based on token, sequence, and KV cache memory limits. Another common design mixes prefill and decode tokens within the same batch (piggybacking), allowing ongoing generation to advance while new prompts are processed, which reduces long interruptions between decode steps (Agrawal et al., 2023; 2024). We use the phase-separated design to keep decode batches homogeneous, making the throughput effects of early exit easier to isolate. The CDB method itself does not require phase separation and could also be combined with piggybacking. Chunked prefill. Generation begins with prefill, which processes the prompt and writes the resulting attention keys and values to the KV cache. Since all prompt tokens are known in advance, they can be processed in parallel. We pack the prompts of multiple requests into prefill batch containing at most tokens (Fig. 8, left). If prompt does not fit into the remaining batch budget, we process the part that fits and continue the remaining tokens in the next prefill batch. This chunked prefill bounds the work of each prefill batch and prevents single long prompt from occupying the GPU in one large forward pass. Once the final prompt token has been processed, its output produces the first generated token and the sequence enters decode. Decode is autoregressive: each generated token becomes the input for the next step, so every sequence advances by only one token at time (Fig. 8, left). Paged KV cache. During generation, each sequence continuously extends its KV cache with the keys and values of newly processed tokens, so its memory footprint grows. The caches of all active sequences share the limited GPU memory, which bounds the size of the active set and thus the achievable decode batch size. Output lengths are unknown in advance and memory requirements of sequences may differ substantially. Reserving space for the maximum possible length of every sequence would admit only small active set and result in small decode batches. We use paged KV cache (Kwon et al., 2023), which divides the cache into fixed-size blocks and assigns new blocks as sequence grows (Fig. 8, right). This incremental allocation uses the available capacity efficiently, although the cache may still fill before generation finishes, which requires preemption policy. Preemption. The scheduler admits new requests only while sufficient cache capacity is available. If active sequences nevertheless exhaust the KV-cache capacity because they generate more tokens than expected, the scheduler can remove an active sequence by releasing its KV blocks and returning it to the waiting set. We implement two preemption policies. Offloading moves the KV state to CPU memory and restores it when the sequence resumes, preserving the values produced during decode. Depth-adaptive decoding applies early-exit only during decode, while prefill always runs at full depth. Tokens that originally exited early are therefore processed again at full depth, so their reconstructed KV values may differ from those produced during decode. Although this repeats model computation, prefill processes the known tokens in parallel and is much faster per token than autoregressive decode, making cache reconstruction relatively efficient. A.2 BATCHING AND ADMISSION PARAMETERS Table 1 summarizes the configuration used in our main experiments, and the following paragraphs explain the parameters that control batching and admission. Maximum batch sizes. GPU memory limits how many sequences and tokens can be batched together. Model parameters occupy fixed part of this memory, while the remaining capacity is primarily shared between the KV cache and intermediate activations. We therefore use sequence limit (max num sequences) and token limit (max num batched tokens). The KV cache grows with the number and length of active sequences, so limits how many sequences may retain KV state on the GPU. Since each active sequence contributes only one token during decode, also defines the maximum decode batch size (Fig. 8, left). In Section 6.2, we vary (and thus the decode batch size) to evaluate CDB in memoryand compute-bound regimes. During prefill, limits the total number of prompt tokens batched together. Since > in our experiments, the token limit does not further restrict decode batches. larger allows more prompt tokens to be processed together, which requires more activation memory and may interrupt decode for longer. Prefill admission. The active set contains at most sequences. When sequences finish, they free slots that can be filled by new sequences. Because prefill and decode run in separate batches, filling these slots requires prefill batch, which temporarily pauses decode. Refilling each slot immediately can produce many prefill batches containing only one or few prompts. However, prefill uses the GPU efficiently once batch contains enough tokens to become compute-bound. sufficiently long prompt can reach this regime by itself, so waiting to combine it with other prompts gives little throughput benefit. Short prompts may not contain enough tokens, making it more efficient to wait for several free slots to combine more prompts. For example, the short Alpaca prompts generally require more sequences to form compute-bound prefill batch than the longer ShareGPT prompts. The min free slots parameter makes the scheduler wait until chosen number of slots are free before interrupting decode for prefill. low value can cause frequent and inefficient prefill interruptions, while high value makes decode less efficient as the decode batch shrinks with less active sequences. KV-cache headroom. The memory footprint of the KV cache depends on the prompt and generated lengths of each active sequence. The maximum number of sequences therefore provides only coarse control over memory use. The KV-cache headroom ρKV specifies how much of the cache should remain free so that active sequences can add new KV entries as they generate new tokens. Preprint. When the free capacity falls below this value, the scheduler stops admitting new sequences and continues decoding the active set. For example, two sequences with very long prompts may already leave less free cache than the configured headroom, even if =64. The scheduler then keeps the active set at two until one finishes and releases its KV state. The KV-cache headroom therefore adapts the active-set size to its actual memory use, while provides fixed upper bound. Many of these operations are executed by separate GPU kernels that the CPU normally launches individually. The small overhead of each launch accumulates across layers and sequences. We reduce this launch overhead with CUDA graphs, which record sequence of GPU operations once and replay it with little CPU involvement. The recorded operations, tensor shapes, and tensor memory addresses must remain fixed between replays, only the values stored in the tensors may change. We therefore preallocate reusable input and output buffers whose contents are updated for each batch. To support different batch sizes, we pad batches to set of supported buckets and capture the corresponding graphs during warm-up. For CB, each graph captures the complete decode forward pass. For CDB, we capture separate graphs for the 19 Preprint. prelude, recurrent core, and coda because the scheduler executes these stages independently. Both engines capture prefill separately from decode. In prefill, the attention operation depends on how prompt tokens are divided among sequences, which determines which tokens attend to one another. Capturing separate compute graph for every possible combination of prompt lengths would be infeasible. We therefore break the prefill graph at each attention operation following SGLang. Attention and output projection. We use FlashAttention-3 for both prefill and decode (Shah et al., 2024). Prefill uses its variable-length (varlen) path, and decode uses its fast path for paged KV caches. The output projection over the vocabulary can also be expensive for large prefill batches. Only the final token of completed prompt produces generated token, so we compute output logits only for these positions instead of for every prompt token. sections.title: INPUT AND OUTPUT TOKENS
sections.content: Figure 10: Empirical CDFs of prompt (left) and output (right) token lengths for the three workloads under the Ouro tokenizer. In our experiments, we do not let the models generate their own responses, as they may deviate between runs. Instead, we take prompt and reference-output lengths from the ShareGPT (ShareGPT Team, 2023), Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023), and ArXiv-Summarization (Cohan et al., 2018) datasets. From ShareGPT we take one request per conversation by using the first user-assistant pair, so each request is single-turn. For Alpaca we pair each instruction with its reference output, and for ArXiv we do the same for each article and its corresponding abstract. We tokenize every prompt and reference output with each models tokenizer, drop pairs with fewer than four prompt or output tokens, and drop requests whose combined length exceeds the context length of 16,384 tokens. All tested models replay the same requests in the same order. Only small differences in token lengths arise from their different tokenizers. This leaves 56,067 ShareGPT, 49,443 Alpaca, and 11,899 ArXiv requests. The offline threshold sweeps replay 6,000 ShareGPT, 10,000 Alpaca, and 1,000 ArXiv requests. The reported throughput is stable at these sample sizes, and running more requests would only increase experiment duration. For the serving experiments, each point replays fixed 10-minute Poisson arrival trace, so its request count is determined by the offered request rate. Fig. 10 shows the resulting input and output token length distributions under the Ouro tokenizer (Zhu et al., 2025). Alpaca requests are short and tightly concentrated (mean prompt and output lengths of 18 and 60 tokens), whereas ShareGPT requests are long and heavy-tailed (mean 267 and 311 tokens, with 99th prompt-length percentile of 3264 tokens against Alpacas 75). ArXiv provides prefill-heavy workload: its mean prompt and output lengths are 6,989 and 370 tokens, with medians of 6,436 and 199 tokens. Its prompts are approximately 26 longer than ShareGPTs on average, while its outputs are only 1.2 and 5.2 longer. ShareGPT prompts and outputs are in turn on average 14.8 longer than Alpacas. C.2 EARLY-EXIT DISTRIBUTION Similar to the output tokens, we do not use an active exit gate during our experiments. To make exit decisions deterministic, we run all requests through the models once in advance and record their per-token exits, which are then replayed during the experiments. Fig. 11 shows the resulting exit-depth distributions for different gate thresholds for Ouro and Huginn. For Ouro, higher gate threshold makes fewer tokens exit early; for Huginn, lower convergence threshold has the same effect. Across all three workloads, the exit-depth distributions remain similar at given threshold, with only modest workload-dependent shifts. Huginns convergence gate spreads exits over wider range of depths than Ouros gate. Preprint. Figure 11: Exit-depth distributions for different gate thresholds. ACCURACY-EFFICIENCY TRADE-OFF ABLATIONS Our work is about maximizing the inference efficiency of looped LMs. This section evaluates how well current models support the techniques we build on. We reimplement the gsm8k_cot task configuration of the LM Evaluation Harness (Cobbe et al., 2021; Sutawika et al., 2026) on top of our continuous-batching and continuous-depth-batching implementations, and evaluate Ouro 1.4B (Zhu et al., 2025) and Huginn 3.5B (Geiping et al., 2025). Two choices in our setup affect task accuracy: the KV cache policy and the exit gate, both trading off accuracy against throughput and memory. E.1 KV CACHE SHARING Looped LMs share physical attention layers across iterations, so multiple iterations can also share KV cache slots. Neither model was trained for this setting, so KV sharing is zero-shot capability here. We test how KV cache sharing affects accuracy and memory, evaluating both models at fixed depth. We compare full depth-indexed cache, where each loop iteration writes to its own KV slot, against two shared layouts: single-slot, where every iteration overwrites one shared KV slot per physical layer, and first-then-shared, where the first iteration retains private slot while all subsequent ones share second. Writing for the number of KV slots per recurrent layer, the three layouts use = rmax, = 1, and = 2, respectively. The total cache thus holds ℓ0 + ℓrs KV entries per token, where ℓ0 denotes the number of attention layers outside the loop (prelude and coda) and ℓr those inside the recurrent core. Sharing therefore saves factor of ℓ0+ℓrrmax over the depth-indexed cache. ℓ0+ℓrs The results in Table 4 show that the Huginn model is insensitive to the KV sharing layout, while Ouro loses accuracy under both layouts, from about 6 points under first-then-shared to complete collapse under single-slot sharing. We cannot reproduce the results from the Ouro paper, which reports near-lossless KV sharing (Zhu et al., 2025). This might be because they share only during decoding and keep depth-indexed cache for the prompt. Still, they report degradation of about 10 accuracy points once the sharing extends to prefill, which is far less than the drop we observe. 23 Preprint. Our results are in line with Vendrell et al. (2026), who propose integrating KV sharing into Ouros training as solution, which then recovers most of the gap. Surprisingly, Huginn actually performs better under single-slot sharing. Under truncated loop (i.e., reducing rmax), single-slot sharing retains substantially more accuracy than the full depth-indexed cache: 11.45% against 3.71% at depth 6 and 25.25% against 12.43% at depth 9, converging to within about two points at depth 16  (Table 5)  . The simplest strategy is to reduce the fixed depth uniformly for all tokens together. In contrast, depth-adaptive decoding can allocate compute per token, looping less for easy tokens and more for hard ones. We evaluate whether early-exit gating outperforms fixed-depth decoding, and whether the delayed exit decision required by our asynchronous CDB scheduler (Section 4.3) degrades accuracy. Setup. Ouro includes trained exit gate, which we use as the baseline. Since our asynchronous CDB scheduler requires the exit decision one step before the actual exit (Section 4.3), we train two additional exit gates on the frozen model: lookahead gate, which predicts the exit one step in advance, and pre-loop gate, which predicts the exit before the loop starts. Both are trained via gate distillation on Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 (Nathawani et al., 2025; NVIDIA, 2025). Huginn includes no gate, so we adopt the training-free convergence criterion of Geiping et al. (2025), which exits once the normalized L2 distance between consecutive loop states falls below threshold. The threshold direction differs: for Huginn larger value triggers more exits, for Ouro smaller one. For Ouro, we set rmin=2, as the model is not trained to produce useful outputs after single iteration (Zhu et al., 2025). For Huginn, we set rmax=16 rather than the trained 32, since accuracy is flat above 16, and use the shared KV cache layout (single-slot) for better performance (Appendix E.1). Results. Fig. 14 summarizes the results. Depth-adaptive decoding Pareto-dominates fixed depth, reaching higher accuracy at every mean recurrent depth. Ouro performs well down to mean depth 8. The exit distributions in the right panel show that Ouro spreads of tokens over three of its four depths and Huginn over four to seven of its sixteen. 2.5 and Huginn down to Preprint. Regarding delayed exits, the trained lookahead gate closely matches the exit behavior of the teacher gate, achieving approximately the same accuracy and threshold curves. Thus, the exit can be predicted one step earlier just as well as in the same step, validating our scheduler design. Predicting the exit before the loop starts would give the scheduler even more flexibility, but the pre-loop gate does not perform well, confirming the observation of Bae et al. (2025b). For Huginn, the delayed exit decision requires only threshold recalibration and also incurs no accuracy cost. Overall, gating is effective for both models, and our delayed exits do not degrade accuracy. However, the minimum loop count remains 2 for the trained gate and 3 for the convergence criterion (which compares two consecutive latent states, plus the additional step from the delayed scheduler), limiting the exit distribution and the compute savings. Ouro and Huginn naturally fit our setup, as they do not exit at those depths, but shallower looped LMs might be more constrained.
